title: Amnesty International Calls for Abolishing ICE for First Time, Citing Unlawful Killings and Abuse
detail: Amnesty International released a 168-page report on Thursday, September 24, 2026 — titled 'We Had Whistles, They Had Guns: Human Rights Violations in U.S. Immigration Enforcement Operations and the Case to Abolish ICE' — documenting alleged human rights violations by ICE, CBP, and other federal agencies during militarized enforcement surges in Chicago, Minneapolis-St. Paul, New Orleans, and Washington, D.C. It is the first time the organization has called for abolishing a U.S. government agency. Researchers interviewed 154 people affected by the operations between March and June 2026, documenting seven incidents involving lethal force — including three alleged unlawful killings (Renee Good, Alex Pretti, and Silverio Villegas González) and the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, whose case has led to federal charges against the ICE officer involved — plus allegations of discriminatory detentions based on race or national origin, and violent repression of peaceful protest. Amy Fischer, Amnesty International USA's director for refugee and migrant rights, said, 'The last thing we need in this country is more cruelty at the hands of ICE and CBP.' The report also opposes the $70 billion ICE/CBP reconciliation package and a planned new family detention center in Alexandria, Louisiana. The White House dismissed the report as 'smears' intended to vilify ICE officers, and a DHS spokesperson responded by citing the criminal records of individuals detained in Chicago rather than addressing the specific allegations.

title: Federal Judge Issues Permanent Injunction Over 'Dreadful' ICE Detention Conditions at 26 Federal Plaza
detail: U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan issued a 127-page permanent injunction on Thursday, September 24, 2026, in a class action brought by Make the Road New York against ICE's detention conditions at 26 Federal Plaza in Lower Manhattan. Kaplan found detainees were held in 'dreadful' and 'squalid' conditions — jammed into holding rooms far beyond capacity, sleeping upright or next to toilets, denied adequate food, water, medical care, and legal counsel — and that ICE had 'intentionally concealed or recklessly disregarded the truth' about its compliance with his prior orders, calling the treatment 'inhumane and unconstitutional' and designed to 'inflict punishment on detainees and induce them to self-deport.' Internal ICE emails cited in the ruling described monkeypox and tuberculosis outbreaks at the facility, with one official writing, 'This week has been one gross contagion after another.' The permanent order requires ICE to cap occupancy at one detainee per 50 square feet, provide clean bedding and hygiene supplies within a day of intake, on-site medical screening before placement in holding rooms, private attorney phone access within 24 hours (with a first legal call within one hour), pillows, and dimmed nighttime lighting. DHS did not immediately comment.

title: DOJ Tries to Deport Peruvian Man to Central African Republic Hours After Appeals Court Blocked Third-Country Removals
detail: A Department of Justice attorney asked a federal judge late Wednesday, September 24, 2026 to lift a stay blocking the transfer of a Peruvian man out of Massachusetts so ICE could move him to another facility 'to effectuate his removal' to the Central African Republic — a country he has never been to — despite a September 18, 2026 ruling from a three-judge panel of the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upholding a lower court's finding that the administration's 'third-country removal' program violated the law. The man had previously been granted Convention Against Torture protection barring his removal to Peru. After an emergency filing from his attorneys, the appeals court wrote just before midnight that, 'consistent with this court's September 18, 2026, Judgment, the March 16, 2026, stay pending appeal is dissolved,' blocking the transfer. DHS General Counsel James Percival argued 'the third country deportation policy continues, as the First Circuit's ruling is not currently in effect,' while Immigration Litigation Alliance executive director Trina Realmuto said the administration 'refused to acknowledge that they lost in court' and 'came up with this technical point' to keep pursuing the removal. Acting Associate Attorney General nominee testimony aside, DOJ has said it intends to appeal the underlying ruling.
